extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in dramatic and poetic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging or producing dramatic and poetic works (tragedy, comedy, verse, and translation), emphasizing language, characterization, structure, moral effect, and fidelity in translation. Draws on contrasts between Shakespeare/Molière/ancients and contemporary sentimental or French drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness of parts and harmony of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: "Preserving a fitness in the parts, and a harmony in the whole, they form a nature of their own..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should show internal coherence: parts should fit together and contribute to an overall artistic unity. This kind of consistency creates a distinctive ‘nature’ for the piece and enables it to stimulate active thought and a striving after ideal excellence. Anti-pattern: disjointed plays where scenes or devices are inconsistent with the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of language and transitions in passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the "perpetual falsification of the language, and of the connections and transitions of thought, which Nature has appropriated to states of passion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue and emotional transitions must feel natural to states of passion; do not force artificial phrases, slangy or stock expressions, or contrived transitions that falsify how people actually feel or move between feelings. Such falsification undermines dramatic verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should elevate and transport the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic scenes should "transport the mind to a sense of its possible greatness, and to implant the germs of that greatness... suspending our individual recollections and lulling them to sleep amid the music of nobler thoughts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim of high tragedy is to raise the spectator's imagination and understanding, not merely to produce sensation or mimic ordinary suffering. Work should cultivate a feeling of nobility and intellectual engagement rather than wallowing in private detail alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: "Aristotle... required of the poet an involution of the universal in the individual."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great characters embody universal truths while remaining particular and individual. The writer should show the universal (moral, psychological truth) through a distinct individual form, not by abstract generalizing nor by flat type-characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character individualization and instructiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Class-characteristics must be "so modified and particularized in each person... that life itself does not excite more distinctly that sense of individuality which belongs to real existence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable class- or type-traits as starting material but particularize them richly so each character feels unique and instructive. Examples cited: Jaques, Falstaff, fools and clowns of Shakespeare, or Molière’s Miser—they teach general truths by being vividly particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must spring from natural human growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous qualities in Shakespeare and Molière are "the natural growth of the human mind" and thus transferable to the reader's own heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should arise from believable human traits and situations, not from cheap physical gags, ephemeral slang, or artificial exaggerations. Aim for laughter that deepens understanding rather than mere momentary amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mawkish sentimentalism and hypocritical moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern sentimental plays are described as filled with Christian morality that can be "exercised without a single Christian virtue..."—adulation that flatters the audience and sends them away pleased with their own hearts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not offer facile, self-congratulatory moral lessons that require no sacrifice or genuine virtue. Avoid cheap pathos ('maudlin tears') and moral posturing that flatters rather than challenges the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manner, language, and situation over mere plot novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of audiences who seek in a tragedy the same gratification they get from the new novel: "the only curiosity, we feel, is in the story..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's manner—its language, the action/reaction of the passions, the shaping of situations—matters more than merely surprising plot points. Even familiar stories can be great if handled with distinctive style and depth; conversely, a novel plot cannot substitute for poor manner or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance emotional effect with intellectual engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic scenes should affect us "within the bounds of pleasure, and in union with the activity both of our understanding and imagination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional impact should not numb the intellect; aim for feelings that coexist with thoughtful imagination. Avoid pure sensation that stupefies the audience—pleasurable emotion must be coupled with cognitive and imaginative activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding vice or subverting the moral order for mere surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The "secret of dramatic popularity" often lies in "the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things... rewarding with all the sympathies those criminals whom law, reason, and religion have excommunicated from our esteem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of cheap devices that win sympathy for immoral characters simply to shock or surprise. Dramatic interest should not depend on unjustly reversing moral consequences; maintain moral plausibility unless you deliberately and thoughtfully investigate moral ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let spectacle overshadow dramatic substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote of a deafening explosion and gunpowder smell so strong "the naturalness of the scene was quite astonishing!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage effects and sensational physical tricks can dazzle but should not substitute for well-wrought drama. Use spectacle sparingly and ensure it serves the narrative and emotional truth rather than drowning the play’s substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank verse: prioritize pauses, cadences, and paragraph sweep
rubrics_metrics.description: "Harmonious verse... apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs, 'with many a winding bout / Of linked sweetness long drawn out,' and not in the even flow... nor in the prominence of antithetic vigour of single lines..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In iambic blank verse, favor the shaping of longer cadential passages and flexible pauses that create a flowing paragraphic music. Do not rely on a monotonous even flow or over-emphasize isolated antithetic lines except where a specific dramatic purpose requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and completeness in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the translations had been bad... the English was no translation--there were pages on pages not in the original--and half the original was not to be found in the translation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should faithfully render the original’s content and spirit: avoid omissions, unwarranted additions, or liberties that change meaning. Preserve completeness and accuracy rather than producing a text that misrepresents the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency and dignity in tragic and comic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients and elder dramatists treated comedy and tragedy as kinds of poetry, avoiding low, shop-metaphor language in comedy and maudlin pathos in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the dignity appropriate to each register: comedy can be comic without descending to slang or grotesque distortions; tragedy should not pander to base sympathies. Tone should be consistent with the poetic and moral aims of the piece.
